statement: A vector space (or linear space) over a field F is a set V whose elements (vectors) can be added together and multiplied ("scaled") by numbers called scalars (elements of F), subject to vector addition and scalar multiplication satisfying the vector axioms.

symbols.meaning: field of scalars (such as R or C)

properties.property: Any vector space over a given field is characterized, up to isomorphism, by its dimension
properties.why: linear algebra completely classifies vector spaces over a given field by their dimension

properties.property: The addition operation allows only finitely many terms to be added
properties.why: linear algebra per se is not adapted to deal with infinite series without additional structure

properties.property: Real and complex vector spaces are kinds of vector spaces based on real numbers and complex numbers
properties.why: scalars can be elements of any field, commonly chosen to be R or C

assumptions.assumption: Scalars are elements of a field F
assumptions.breaks_when: The scalar algebraic structure is not a field

assumptions.assumption: Vector operations are restricted to finite algebraic combinations
assumptions.breaks_when: Formulating infinite series or limits without endowing the space with a compatible topology

failure_modes.signature: Limits of vector sequences and infinite sums cannot be evaluated
failure_modes.cause: A vector space per se lacks a topology or notion of vectors being close to each other

failure_modes.mode: Inability to measure lengths or angles
failure_modes.signature: Vector magnitudes, distances, and angles are undefined
failure_modes.cause: The vector space is not endowed with additional data such as a norm or an inner product
